● The lighthouse on Carrow Point had stood for a hundred and twelve years, and for the last thirty of them Elias
  Wren had kept its lamp. He climbed the iron stairs every evening at dusk, one hundred and forty-seven steps,
  and every morning he climbed down again. In between, he wound the clockwork, trimmed the wick, polished the
  great lens until the glass held no fingerprints, and wrote the weather in a ledger that nobody read.

  The ledger was the only thing he had kept from his father, who had kept the light before him. The first page
  was filled with a careful copper-plate hand that recorded wind from the northwest, fog in the early hours, a
  schooner lost off the eastern reef in the autumn of 1931. Elias had continued the record in his own cramped
  handwriting, and sometimes he turned back through the pages in the long winter nights just to hear the rhythm
  of the entries, the small daily facts that added up to a life.
